text:
The University of Chicago's history began with the founding of the Old University of Chicago in 1857, which closed in 1886. A new University of Chicago was incorporated in 1890, supported by donations from John D. Rockefeller and Marshall Field. William Rainey Harper became president in 1891, and the institution adopted the quarter system. The university's identity evolved significantly under subsequent presidents; Robert Maynard Hutchins became president in 1929 and implemented the "New Plan" curriculum.
Academically, the university is structured around a college, four divisions of graduate research, seven professional schools, and the Graham School of Continuing Liberal and Professional Studies. It is classified as an "R1: Doctoral University – Very high research activity." The main campus spans 217 acres in Hyde Park and Woodlawn. Notable academic achievements include playing a role in shaping the Chicago school of economics and the Chicago school of sociology, and hosting the site of Chicago Pile-1. The University of Chicago also maintains satellite campuses abroad, including in Hong Kong, London, and Paris.
